content_voiceover: Pure red cell aplasia is a normochromic, macrocytic anemia with severe reticulocytopenia under one percent, and bone marrow showing erythroblasts absent or under one percent — everything else in the marrow is normal. About forty percent of cases have a circulating erythropoiesis inhibitor in the plasma. For boards, memorize the classification. Congenital causes include Diamond-Blackfan anemia, inherited, with RPS19 or DBA1 mutations found in about twenty-five percent, versus the non-inherited Pearson syndrome. Acquired primary PRCA is usually autoimmune, including transient erythroblastopenia of childhood. The classic secondary association is thymoma, which is T-cell mediated — always screen a new PRCA patient for thymoma with chest imaging. Also link PRCA to hematologic malignancies like CLL, and to infections — the single most important is human parvovirus B19, which directly infects erythroid progenitors via the P antigen receptor; the marrow shows giant pronormoblasts with nuclear inclusions. B19-associated PRCA classically causes transient aplastic crisis in patients with chronic hemolysis, and is treated with IVIG. Other notable secondary causes include post-transplant anti-ABO antibodies and anti-erythropoietin antibodies after EPO therapy. Treatment: stop offending drugs, control infection with IVIG for parvovirus, replace B12 and folate, thymectomy for thymoma-associated cases with about forty percent response, and immunosuppression — prednisone, cyclosporine which has the best response rate at sixty-five to eighty percent, cyclophosphamide or azathioprine, ATG, IVIG, or splenectomy as later options.
keypoints: PRCA = macrocytic anemia, retic <1%, marrow erythroblasts <1%
Thymoma (T-cell mediated) — always screen with imaging
Parvovirus B19 → giant pronormoblasts; Tx = IVIG
